Abstract
With the development of the information age, the security of image data has become increasingly important. To enhance 
image security in applications such as data hiding and privacy protection, this study proposes an innovative encryption 
framework that synergizes a random Zigzag scrambling scheme with a roulette wheel rotation diffusion method. The sys-
tem constructs a novel four-dimensional hyperchaotic model by embedding an additional state variable into a classical 
three-dimensional chaotic structure. The simulation results confirm that the generated chaotic sequences exhibit strong 
hyperchaotic behavior and uniformity across diverse parameter settings. The encryption approach effectively disrupts both 
the pixel positions and intensity values through combined Zigzag path scrambling and rotational diffusion, both of which 
are deeply coupled with the designed chaotic system. Notably, the chaotic system's initial parameters are computed directly 
from the grayscale values of the source image, ensuring that encryption is highly sensitive to both the plaintext and the key, 
thus strengthening security. The performance evaluation indicates that the method offers an expansive key space on the scale 
of ­2384 × ­1060, while the entropy of the encrypted image reaches 7.9993 bits per pixel. Furthermore, the algorithm achieves 
a normalized pixel change rate (NPCR) of 99.6048% and a unified average changing intensity (UACI) of 33.4706%, dem-
onstrating strong resistance to statistical attacks and robustness against cropping and noise-based tampering. Overall, the 
method delivers a high level of encryption performance with notable resilience.

1  Introduction
With the continuous development of computing technology 
and multimedia communication, the volume of data 
generated, shared, and stored—such as images, videos, and 
audio—has grown significantly, especially across fields such 
as e-commerce, healthcare, and national defense. Despite 
the convenience of cloud services, digital images remain 
vulnerable to various forms of cyber threats, including data 
theft, tampering, and forgery. Such attacks not only infringe 
on personal privacy but can also trigger substantial financial 
and reputational losses. Consequently, there is an increasing 
demand for robust and efficient image security mechanisms. 
Conventional image encryption algorithms often suffer from 
limited efficiency (Wang et al. 2015; SaberiKamarposhti 
et al. 2024), underscoring the need for improved solutions 
in this domain.
Chaotic system-based encryption techniques have 
demonstrated superior performance compared with 
traditional methods, attracting widespread academic interest 
(Xu et al. 2025; Alexan et al. 2025; Özpolat et al. 2025; 
Darani et al. 2024). Matthews pioneered the introduction 
of chaotic dynamics into cryptographic systems as early as 
1989, laying the foundation for the concept of chaos-based 
encryption (Matthews 1989). Subsequently, Lu enhanced the 
sine map to construct a modified chaotic system capable of 
increasing both the randomness and unpredictability of the 
cipher process (Lu et al. 2024). Although one-dimensional 
chaotic systems offer structural simplicity and lower 
implementation complexity, they are often constrained by 
narrow chaotic ranges, which can result in a nonuniform 
sequence distribution and compromised encryption

tend to generate more complex and widely spread chaotic 
sequences, improving the overall encryption Quality. For 
example, Ma developed both 2D and 3D logical cosine 
cascade maps (2D-LCCM and 3D-LCCM), successfully 
applying them to the scrambling and diffusion stages of 
encryption. These mappings enhance both the security 
and computational efficiency (Yu et al. 2023). Similarly, 
Zhang introduced a hybrid Lorenz–Sine chaotic model 
featuring multiple symmetric singular attractors and a broad 
chaotic domain. Building on this, a helicoidal rotation- 
based encryption scheme was devised, offering high 
resistance against differential analysis (Zhang et al. 2023). 
Furthermore, Lai presented a novel two-dimensional chaotic 
mapping model for image encryption, which has been shown 
through experimental evaluations to exhibit stronger chaotic 
behavior and better resistance to noise and cropping than 
earlier one-dimensional approaches did (Lai et al. 2023).
The application of Zigzag transformation in image 
encryption is also common, and many researchers have pro-
posed numerous image encryption schemes based on Zigzag 
transformation (Zhang and Wang 2023; Wang et al. 2022a, 
b; Li et al. 2022). Zhang proposed a new three-dimensional 
transformed Zigzag diffusion algorithm, which arranged 
the plaintext image pixel values into a cube shape and uti-
lized pseudorandom matrices for Zigzag diffusion capable 
of resisting different types of attacks (Zhang et al. 2021). 
Wang combined the extended Zigzag transformation with 
RNA computation to propose a new encryption scheme. 
This not only solved the problem of certain elements always 
remaining in the same position in each encryption round 
but also ensured that the encoding rules of the RNA matrix 
were completely controlled by chaotic sequences, making 
the computation results more difficult to predict. Experi-
mental results have shown that this encryption algorithm has 
very high security performance (Wang and Guan 2020). Li 
proposed a three-dimensional chaotic mapping-based Zig-
zag encryption scheme for color images. Experiments have 
shown that the method has strong resistance to brute force 
and statistical attacks but lacks differential attack analysis 
(Li et al. 2015). Wang improved the Zigzag transform by 
changing the starting point and direction and dividing the 
pixel matrix into upper and lower triangles, scrambling them 
according to different Zigzag transform methods, and experi-
mental analysis revealed that the scheme has better security 
(Wang and Chen 2021).
Pixel-level scrambling alone can only change the pixel 
position. To enhance encryption performance, many 
researchers have proposed bit-level scrambling algorithms 
(Man et al. 2023; Zhu et al. 2023; Wei et al. 2023; Chen 
et al. 2022a). Xu treated the image as a three-dimensional 
bit matrix and used the Latin cube for diffusion and scram-
bling. By combining three-dimensional bit matrices with 
Latin cubes, the method achieves both high security and high 
efficiency (Xu and Tian 2019). Wen processed the image bit 
planes separately, with bit-level substitution in the higher 
4-bit planes and exclusive OR (XOR) diffusion in the lower 
4-bit planes, which has low computational complexity but 
is not secure against selective plaintext attacks and is easily 
cracked (Wen and Yu 2019).
The diffusion stage plays a vital role in enhancing image 
encryption by improving randomness and unpredictability 
(Chai et al. 2024; Ding et al. 2024; Yan et al. 2025). Wang 
proposed an enhanced Zigzag strategy that performs bit-
level scrambling on image subblocks, followed by a linewise 
diffusion process. While this method effectively alters pixel 
values, its unidirectional nature renders it relatively simple 
in structure (Wang et al. 2021). In another approach, Liu 
integrated improved DNA encoding with a fast diffusion 
mechanism, employing matrix and vector operations across 
RGB channels in a three-dimensional six-directional man-
ner. Although the resulting scheme exhibited strong security 
performance, its encryption speed was relatively low (Liu 
et al. 2023). Additionally, Hussain Muhammad introduced 
a method using diagonal and antidiagonal dislocations for 
pixel diffusion in a parallelized structure, leading to efficient 
processing (Hussain et al. 2022). Nevertheless, its fixed-
order processing of pixels compromises the randomness 
of encryption, increasing its vulnerability to analysis and 
attack. This underscores the need for more sophisticated and 
randomized diffusion techniques.
Building upon these insights, this paper presents a novel 
four-dimensional chaotic system that evolved from the Lor-
enz model and integrates it into an encryption framework 
that leverages randomly selected Zigzag mappings and a 
roulette wheel-based rotational coding strategy. Initially, the 
system’s chaotic parameters are dynamically generated from 
the plaintext image values, improving the scheme’s sensitiv-
ity to both the input content and the secret key and thereby 
strengthening the encryption robustness. Next, the pixel 
locations are scrambled via the proposed Zigzag approach, 
where small image blocks are randomly selected and their 
size varies dynamically to enhance disruption. Afterward, 
both pixel-level and bit-level scrambling are performed, 
achieving dual-layer disorder and significantly weakening 
the statistical relevance between neighboring pixels. In the 
final encryption stage, the ciphertext undergoes a roulette 
wheel-guided rotation-based diffusion process, followed 
by a two-directional, nonlinear scrambling phase that sig-
nificantly enhances the overall randomness and diffusion 
strength.
The main contributions of this work are as follows:
(1)	 A four-dimensional hyperchaotic system is constructed, 
featuring uniformly distributed trajectories, hypercha-
otic dynamics, and extensive parameter flexibility,

2  Basic knowledge
2.1  Zigzag transformation
The zigzag transformation is a pixel rearrangement 
technique that traverses a two-dimensional image matrix in 
a predefined pattern and converts it into a one-dimensional 
sequence. Specifically, the traversal begins at the upper-
left corner of the matrix, following a pattern that alternates 
between vertical and diagonal movements until all the 
pixels have been visited. The pixel values are then extracted 
according to this traversal path and reordered into a one-
dimensional sequence. This sequence can subsequently 
be reshaped back into a matrix for further processing. 
Figure 1 illustrates the result of applying the standard zigzag 
transformation.

3.2  Exponential and bifurcated Lyapunov diagrams
The Lyapunov exponent (LE) is a core metric used to assess 
the dynamic stability and chaotic nature of systems. It 
was introduced by the Russian mathematician Alexander 
Lyapunov in the late nineteenth century (Wang et al. 2024). 
In general, if the largest LE of a system is positive, the 
system exhibits chaos. If more than one LE is positive, 
the system is considered hyperchaotic, indicating more 
complex and unpredictable behavior. As shown in Fig. 4, 
the calculated Lyapunov spectrum for the proposed system 
under parameters a = 15.5, b = 50, c = 3.6, and d = 0.2, with

yields LE1 = 1.3208, LE2 = 0.2140, LE3 = − 9.0862, and 
LE4 = − 21.5302. This confirms the presence of hyperchaotic 
dynamics, with two positive exponents indicating strong 
sensitivity and irregularity.

conditions—minute changes can lead to diverging 
trajectories over time. To verify this, Fig. 6 presents the

diverge rapidly owing to exponential error growth—a 
hallmark of chaotic behavior. This observation verifies the 
system’s extreme sensitivity and supports its applicability 
in cryptographic contexts where unpredictability and key

3.5  NIST statistical test
The NIST test suite is widely used to evaluate the random-
ness properties of binary sequences generated by pseudor-
andom number generators (Bassham et al. 2010). In this 
work, to verify the randomness of sequences derived from 
the proposed four-dimensional hyperchaotic system, suffi-
ciently long numerical sequences were first generated and 
then converted into binary bitstreams.
These sequences were subjected to the full NIST SP800-
22 test suite, and the outcomes—summarized in Table 2—
demonstrate that the generated bitstreams pass all test items 
successfully. This confirms that the chaotic system exhibits 
strong statistical randomness and is suitable for crypto-
graphic applications.

4  Encryption scheme
The proposed encryption algorithm begins by generating a 
key via the SHA-384 algorithm, which is subsequently used 
to initialize and iterate a four-dimensional chaotic system, 
yielding four chaotic sequences. These sequences serve as 
the basis for a series of image transformation operations. 
The plaintext image first undergoes a Zigzag transformation, 
followed by block-based bit-level scrambling, roulette wheel 
rotation coding, and bidirectional nonsequential diffusion to 
obtain the final encrypted image.

4.4  Encryption procedure
Let the input grayscale image P be of size M × N. where 
M and N denote the image height and width, respectively. 
The proposed encryption algorithm consists of a multistage 
process that combines local permutation, quaternary-domain 
scrambling, and chaotic diffusion strategies. The detailed 
steps are as follows:
Step 1:  Information input. Import the plaintext 
image P along with the externally defined key vector.
Step 2: Key handling. Using the secret key, generate 
the primary chaotic sequences Xʹ, Yʹ, Zʹ, Wʹ and auxil-
iary sequences U and V via the hyperchaotic system, as 
detailed in Section 4.1.
Step 3:  Zigzag transformation. On the basis of 
sequences U and V, 30 coordinate pairs are constructed. 
These coordinates determine the ranges of 30 small 
matrix blocks within the image. Each of these blocks 
undergoes a Zigzag transformation to produce the inter-
mediate matrix P1.
Step 4: Bit-level scrambling. The image is divided into 
2×2 subblocks. The pixel values within each block are 
converted to a Quaternary representation, and bit-cross 
scrambling is applied as described in Section 4.2 to obtain 
the matrix P2.
Step 5: Roulette wheel rotation coding. The roulette 
wheel rotation coding algorithm (detailed in Section 4.3) 
is applied to matrix P2 to perform pixel-level diffusion, 
resulting in matrix P3.
Step 6:  Nonsequential diffusion. Sort the chaotic 
sequence X, generate index matrix Ix. Then, bidirectional 
nonsequential diffusion is applied to P3 via the method 
outlined in Section 4.3. This global diffusion step pro-
duces the final encrypted image C.
The decryption process is performed by reversing the 
encryption steps in the opposite sequence using the same key 
parameters. A flowchart illustrating the complete encryption 
process is presented in Fig. 13.

5.10  Known‑plaintext attack
To further verify the security of the proposed encryption 
algorithm, we evaluated its resistance against known-plain-
text attacks (KPA)((Qu et al. 2024, 2021)). It is assumed 
that the attacker possesses a pair of plaintext-ciphertext 
images ­(P1 and ­C1) and attempts to use this information to 
analyze or crack the encryption of another image ­(P2 → ­C2). 
During the experiment, the external key was kept fixed to 
simulate the attacker's ability to obtain multiple pairs of 
encrypted image samples under the same key settings in 
real-world scenarios.
In this experiment, standard test images Boat ­(P1) and 
Peppers ­(P2) were selected, and the two images were 
completely irrelevant in content. We first normalize the 
plaintext and ciphertext images to the [0, 1] interval and 
plot their pixel scatter plots to analyze the statistical 
relationship between them(Lu et al. 2025). As shown in 
Fig. 24, the plaintext and ciphertext pixel points are in 
a completely disordered distribution on the plane, with 
no obvious functional or correlation structure, indicating 
that the encryption algorithm can effectively disrupt the 
statistical characteristics of the plaintext.
Furthermore, to analyze the similarity between images 
quantitatively, we calculate the structural similarity 
index (SSIM) between the plaintext and the correspond-
ing ciphertext. The results are SSIM(P1, ­C1) = 0.0000 and 
SSIM(P2, ­C2) = –0.0011. These results indicate that even 
when the same external key is used, almost no useful 
information about the plaintext can be obtained from the 
ciphertext, demonstrating that the proposed algorithm 
has a good ability to resist known-plaintext attacks.
6  Conclusion
This work introduces a novel 4D hyperchaotic system 
that demonstrates extensive chaotic behavior and pre-
sents an image encryption framework that combines ran-
domized Zigzag transformations with roulette wheel dif-
fusion. First, multiple sets of coordinates are generated 
according to the chaotic sequences, the plaintext image 
is then selected on the basis of these coordinates, and the 
resulting small blocks are scrambled in a Zigzag manner. 
Following this, the scrambled pixels are further scram-
bled at the bit level. Next, we apply the roulette wheel 
rotation diffusion algorithm to enhance the encryption 
effect. Finally, the pixel matrix of the image is diffusely 
processed in both directions in a nonsequential man-
ner to achieve global diffusion to obtain the encrypted 
image. The experimental results verify the algorithm's 
capability for complete image encryption/decryption and 
robust defense against diverse attacks, confirming its

Abstract: With the development of the information age, the security of image data has become increasingly important. To enhance image security in applications such as data hiding and privacy protection, this study proposes an innovative encryption framework that synergizes a random Zigzag scrambling scheme with a roulette wheel rotation diffusion method. The sys- tem constructs a novel four-dimensional hyperchaotic model by embedding an additional state variable into a classical three-dimensional chaotic structure. The simulation results confirm that the generated chaotic sequences exhibit strong hyperchaotic behavior and uniformity across diverse parameter settings. The encryption approach effectively disrupts both the pixel positions and intensity values through combined Zigzag path scrambling and rotational diffusion, both of which are deeply coupled with the designed chaotic system. Notably, the chaotic system's initial parameters are computed directly from the grayscale values of the source image, ensuring that encryption is highly sensitive to both the plaintext and the key, thus strengthening security. The performance evaluation indicates that the method offers an expansive key space on the scale of ­2384 × ­1060, while the entropy of the encrypted image reaches 7.9993 bits per pixel. Furthermore, the algorithm achieves a normalized pixel change rate (NPCR) of 99.6048% and a unified average changing intensity (UACI) of 33.4706%, dem- onstrating strong resistance to statistical attacks and robustness against cropping and noise-based tampering. Overall, the method delivers a high level of encryption performance with notable resilience.
